_doc: The 31 named historical deposits (formerly a separate file; every original field kept unchanged, including its lat/lon placeholders tracked by Complaints/281 and its own conf, which describes the grade and share figures) plus three extra ancient sites. surveyed_lat/surveyed_lon give the real location where the deposit is a real named place; ids ending in _generic are placeholders and have none. endowment appears only where it could be justified and is production plus remaining resource, to order of magnitude; endowment_source says how. Entries without an endowment key have none that can be defended. order: position in this file's sequence, so a consumer can list the named deposits in a fixed order (resources by first appearance, deposits within a resource as listed).

entries.name: Elba Hematite
entries.source: Elban hematite is repeatedly named among antiquity's richest and most heavily worked iron ores, mined from surface and near-surface outcrops on Elba since Etruscan times; 500 kg/t (50% Fe) is a round figure for rich, weathered hematite, not an assay of a specific Roman-era working.
entries.surveyed_source: Rio Marina, Elba (Wikipedia names the island 42.8N 10.4E)

entries.name: Noricum Siderite
entries.source: Noricum (the eastern Alps) siderite/limonite ore, the basis of the famous 'Noricum steel' (ferrum Noricum) ancient sources repeatedly praise; 350 kg/t (35% Fe) is a round figure for siderite ore, below its theoretical maximum because real ore always carries gangue.

entries.name: Wealden Bog Iron
entries.source: Wealden clay ironstone and lowland bog iron gathered near the surface rather than mined from a vein - lower grade than Elba's hematite, but requiring far less labour to break out, which is the whole reason bog iron was worth working at all before anyone owned a shaft.
entries.surveyed_source: The Weald, Sussex and Kent; approximate, from memory

entries.name: Hispania Hematite
entries.source: Hematite associated with the oxidised cap of the Iberian Pyrite Belt, the same metallogenic province as the region's copper, lead and silver below; 400 kg/t is a round figure for good-quality hematite, not an assay.

entries.name: North Africa Iron Generic
entries.source: No specific ancient North African iron mine identified by this file's author; a generic mid-range ore-grade placeholder standing in for geography.json's 0.1 regional share so the region is not silently dropped from the supply curve.

entries.name: Anatolian Iron
entries.source: Anatolia is the traditional heartland of early iron metallurgy (Hittite ironworking predates Rome by over a thousand years), so a working iron-ore tradition there by the Roman period is well attested even without a single named mine; 350 kg/t is a round mid-range figure.

entries.name: Levant Iron Generic
entries.source: No specific ancient Levantine/Mesopotamian iron mine identified; generic placeholder for geography.json's 0.05 regional share, same reasoning as north_africa_iron_generic.

entries.name: Italia Copper Generic
entries.source: Minor Etruscan-era copper working in Tuscany/Campania is attested but not at Rio Tinto's scale; generic 3% ore-grade placeholder for geography.json's small 0.02 share.

entries.name: Gaul Germania Copper Generic
entries.source: Generic placeholder; pre-Roman Alpine/Rhineland copper working existed but no single dominant ancient mine identified by this file's author.

entries.name: Britannia Copper Generic
entries.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's 0.05 British copper share.

entries.name: Rio Tinto Copper
entries.source: The Rio Tinto/Iberian Pyrite Belt massive sulfide deposit, one of the largest on Earth, worked to real depth in antiquity - the extensive underground galleries and the drainage-wheel batteries recovered from Roman-era workings there are the standard textbook example of ancient deep hard-rock mining requiring continuous dewatering. 60 kg/t (6% Cu) reflects the richer supergene-enriched zone ancient miners specifically targeted, not the deposit's much lower bulk average grade.
entries.endowment_source: Copper in the Rio Tinto district, production plus resource, order of magnitude from memory; Roman share not separable.
entries.surveyed_source: Riotinto, Huelva; from memory (coordinate known to Wikipedia only for the river)

entries.name: North Africa Copper Generic
entries.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's 0.05 share.

entries.name: Anatolian Copper
entries.source: Anatolia has a copper-working tradition older than bronze itself (native and oxide copper worked since the Chalcolithic); 40 kg/t is a round mid-range figure for a worked oxide/carbonate ore, not an assay of one named mine.

entries.name: Cyprus Copper
entries.source: Cyprus - the island the metal is named after - is worked in antiquity for its oxidised and carbonate copper ores (malachite, azurite, cuprite) in the weathered cap of its ore bodies, cherry-picked at or near the surface long before anyone dug for the much larger but far leaner sulfide ore beneath; 80 kg/t (8%) reflects that enriched cap, not the primary sulfide grade.
entries.endowment_source: Often-quoted order of two hundred thousand tonnes of copper smelted in antiquity, from memory.

entries.name: Italia Lead Generic
entries.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's small 0.02 Italian lead share.

byproducts.source: Wood 2022 (Archaeometry, read): argentiferous galena carries about 0.2 wt% silver, so 0.002 / 0.866 (lead fraction of PbS) = 2.31 kg of silver per tonne of lead contained. Generic galena of no assayed working, so the generic Wood figure; confidence D. Complaints/291.

entries.name: Gaul Germania Lead Generic
entries.source: Generic placeholder; pre-Roman central European galena working existed but no single dominant ancient mine identified.

entries.name: Britannia Lead
entries.source: Mendip and Pennine galena veins, extensively worked from the earliest years of the Roman occupation (lead ingots (pigs) stamped with imperial ownership survive); 150 kg/t (15%) is a round figure for a good vein-galena ore.

byproducts.source: Wood 2022 (Archaeometry, read): argentiferous galena carries about 0.2 wt% silver, so 0.002 / 0.866 (lead fraction of PbS) = 2.31 kg of silver per tonne of lead contained. British galena is attested as argentiferous but no assay is given, so the generic Wood figure; confidence D. Complaints/291.

entries.name: Hispania Lead
entries.source: Cartagena/Sierra argentiferous galena, the same deep-worked district as rio_tinto_copper; 180 kg/t (18%) is a round figure for a rich galena vein.

byproducts.source: Wood 2022 (Archaeometry, read): argentiferous galena carries about 0.2 wt% silver, so 0.002 / 0.866 (lead fraction of PbS) = 2.31 kg of silver per tonne of lead contained. Applied to the Cartagena argentiferous galena (Strabo 3.2.10); no assay of the working itself. Complaints/291.

entries.name: Laurion Lead
entries.source: Laurion's galena, worked to genuine depth through hundreds of shafts over the Classical and Hellenistic periods; by the Roman era the readily accessible rich ore is long since taken and what remains is leaner and deeper, hence a lower grade than Britain's or Spain's fresher veins.

byproducts.source: Laurion ore at about 400 g of silver per tonne with about 20 percent lead (Wood et al., as seen in a search result and not verified in the text read), 400 / 0.20 = 2.0 kg of silver per tonne of lead. Review range 2 to 2.3. Complaints/291.

entries.name: Italia Silver Generic
entries.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's small 0.02 Italian silver share; silver is a trace constituent of argentiferous galena, not its own separate ore.

entries.name: Britannia Silver Generic
entries.source: Silver content of British argentiferous lead ore (see britannia_lead); generic figure, no assay.

entries.name: Hispania Silver
entries.source: Strabo, Geography 3.2.10, citing Polybius, on the silver mines near New Carthage: on the order of 40,000 workers and revenue to Rome of 25,000 drachmas a day - the single best-attested ancient claim of exceptional richness for any deposit in this file. 1.0 kg/t (0.1% Ag) is a correspondingly generous silver content for argentiferous galena, at the rich end of what such ore can carry.

entries.name: Laurion Silver
entries.source: Laurion's silver-lead ore funded the Athenian navy centuries before Rome arrived (Xenophon, Ways and Means, describes the mines at length); by the Roman period the field is old and deep-shafted with its richest ore long extracted, hence a lower silver content than Hispania's fresher workings, not a claim it was ever poor.
entries.endowment_source: Ancient production about 3,000-4,000 t silver (range supplied by project owner).

entries.name: Rio Tinto Jarosite
entries.source: Rio Tinto silver came largely from jarosite and gossan ores smelted with lead added as a collector (Anguilano et al. 2010, ArcheoSciences 34, read). The 0.2 wt% silver grade (2 kg per tonne) is from an abstract seen in a search, not from the paper, and a second independent mention agrees: Bettenay 2022 (Metalla 26.2, supergene-enrichment section, citing Anguilano 2012) gives silver at about 0.2 percent in jarosite ore at the base of the iron cap. Two secondary mentions, primary not opened, so confidence C. The share of the silver-only total is carved from hispania_silver's and is a placeholder: no source gives the split. Surface working in medium rock (gossan is a weathered cap; the hardness is unsourced). Complaints/373.

entries.name: Gaul Germania Tin Generic
entries.source: Generic placeholder for geography.json's small 0.1 share; alluvial cassiterite in Rhine-system gravels, no specific ancient working identified.

entries.name: Cornish Tin Streaming
entries.source: Cornish and Devon 'streaming' of cassiterite (tin ore, dense enough to naturally concentrate in river gravel) is the classic ancient British tin industry, already well known to Mediterranean traders by Herodotus's time; worked with simple ground-sluicing and panning, not the aqueduct-fed hydraulic works Rome later builds for gold at Las Medulas.
entries.endowment_source: Tin metal of the whole Cornwall and Devon district, production plus remaining, order of magnitude from memory; alluvial streaming was the earliest part.

entries.name: Hispania Tin Generic
entries.source: Iberian alluvial cassiterite is attested (geography.json's own located_materials lists hispania among tin's regions) but without a single named ancient working; generic mid-range placer grade.

entries.name: Las Medulas Alluvial
entries.source: Pliny, Natural History 33.66-78, describes the 'ruina montium' method at Las Medulas in detail: aqueducts brought water from many kilometres away to collapse whole hillsides and wash the resulting gravel through sluice channels, which is exactly why this entry's hardness_class is null and its depth_class is 'alluvial_hydraulic' rather than plain 'alluvial' - the labour of BREAKING the ground is done by water, not by hand. 0.0003 kg/t (0.3 g/t) is an order-of-magnitude placer-gold grade typical of a large hydraulic operation, not an assayed figure; share_of_empire_output is this file's own estimate, standing in for the regional breakdown geography.json does not carry for gold - see this file's _doc.
entries.endowment_source: Wikipedia (Las Medulas): 5 million Roman pounds (1.64 million kg) in 250 years, a Pliny-based estimate that is probably generous.

entries.name: Dacia Vein Gold
entries.source: data/world/resources.json's own gold entry names Dacia, opened to Roman exploitation after the conquest of 106 AD, as a second source alongside Las Medulas; the Dacian gold-quartz veins (the Rosia Montana district) are hard-rock epithermal veins worked underground, not placer gravel. 0.008 kg/t (8 g/t) is a typical order-of-magnitude epithermal vein-gold grade, not a specific assay. Region is the free-text label 'dacia': geography.json has no Balkan/Dacian region to key into, so this entry's quantity comes entirely from share_of_empire_output, never from a geography.json lookup - see this file's _doc.
entries.endowment_source: Rosia Montana gold, historic production plus resource, order of magnitude from memory; regional total not known.

entries.name: Almaden Cinnabar
entries.source: Almaden is repeatedly described in the historical-geology literature as among the richest cinnabar (mercury sulfide) deposits ever worked, with ore grades far above the low-single-digit-percent typical of most mercury deposits; 50 kg/t (5% Hg) is a round figure well within its historically reported range, not an assay of a specific Roman-period working. Roman-era exploitation is documented as a convict/damnati-ad-metalla operation under imperial monopoly (see data/world/geography.json's mercury note); depth_class is 'shallow_vein' for the Roman-era workings specifically - the deposit was later worked far deeper, over many further centuries, which is outside this era.
entries.endowment_source: Mercury produced at Almaden over about two thousand years, order of magnitude from memory.

entries.name: Monte Amiata Cinnabar
entries.source: Tuscan (Monte Amiata) cinnabar, worked since Etruscan times, markedly lower grade than Almaden's - this is Complaints/32's own 'about three cinnabar deposits worth working in the Roman world': Almaden and Monte Amiata are the two this file names, both genuinely workable, at very different grades.
entries.endowment_source: Mercury produced at Monte Amiata, order of magnitude from memory.

entries.name: Timna Valley
entries.source: Wikipedia coordinate; one of the oldest copper workings; no endowment figure.

entries.name: Falun
entries.source: Wikipedia coordinate; no endowment figure.

entries.name: Rammelsberg
entries.source: Wikipedia coordinate; no endowment figure.

entries.name: Eastern Desert and Nubian Gold
entries.source: Klemm, Klemm and Murr 2001, Gold of the Pharaohs, J. African Earth Sciences 33, 643-659 (read in full). Quartz-vein ore worked from trenches and shafts: assumed recovery 10 g/t, about two thirds of the maximum concentration mined (p. 658), so 0.010 kg per tonne; tailings kept 3-5 g/t (p. 652). Underground working was limited to about 30 m by the ventilation available to men and oil lamps in New Kingdom workings (p. 654), hence shallow_vein. One entry stands for the whole Eastern Desert and Nubian field (about 250 sites in the paper), placed at the Wadi Allaqi gold district, so the point is a representative position, not a mine. No share_of_empire_output: the paper gives no Roman-era split,, and the entry is catalogue-only like the other entries without a share, so it moves no modelled gold output. Location checked: Wadi Allaqi is named by Klemm as a gold district (Hairiri, Umm Garaiyat) and Wikidata item Q2575777 gives the wadi's mouth near 22.97 N 32.90 E and its centre near 22.5 N 34.0 E; the entry is placed on that line, 22.8 N 33.3 E. Bir Umm Fawakhir was left out because no source opened gave its coordinates.
entries.endowment_source: Klemm et al. 2001, p. 658: maximum total ancient production of 18 t from Predynastic times (about 3000 BC) to about 1350 AD, from 400,000-600,000 t of quartz ore at 10 g/t (at most 6 t) plus wadi workings of the same order or at most double. A ceiling on production, not a resource estimate. About 7 t were Pharaonic; the rest is split equally between Ptolemaic and Arab times.
entries.surveyed_source: Wadi Allaqi, between the two Wikidata Q2575777 positions (22.97 N 32.90 E and 22.5 N 34.0 E)
